props.title: Cléo from 5 to 7

sections.content: Agnès Varda's groundbreaking Cléo from 5 to 7 (1962) revolutionized French New Wave cinema by tracking a pop singer's existential journey through Paris in real-time. Like La Jetée (1962) and Last Year at Marienbad (1961), it experiments radically with time, but Varda's approach feels startlingly immediate and personal. The film's 90-minute runtime (not actually two hours) follows Cléo as she awaits biopsy results, transforming a medical diagnosis into a profound meditation on mortality, femininity, and self-perception.

sections.content: Varda's innovative use of mirrors and reflective surfaces in Cléo creates a complex visual commentary on female objectification that influenced later works like Persona (1966) and 3 Women (1977). The film's structure - divided into numbered chapters - allows Varda to both honor and subvert real-time storytelling. Each segment feels both precise and dreamy, much like Chantal Akerman would later achieve in Jeanne Dielman, 23 Quai du Commerce, 1080 Bruxelles (1975).

The film's exploration of a woman's interior life amidst urban alienation created a template for future character studies like Wanda (1970) and Vagabond (1985). Varda's attention to street life and social observation influenced the development of feminist cinema, setting groundwork for directors like Claire Denis and Kelly Reichardt. sections.content: What sets Cléo apart from its New Wave contemporaries is its distinctly feminine point of view. While films like The 400 Blows (1959) and Band of Outsiders (1964) explored Paris through male protagonists, Varda turns her camera on women's experiences. The film's treatment of Cléo's transformation from object to subject influenced later works like An Angel at My Table (1990) and Portrait of a Lady on Fire (2019).
